questions.q: Where does a dataset's query parameter get mapped to a report parameter's value?
options: On the Parameters tab of the Dataset Properties dialog
In the Report Server's configuration database only
It cannot be viewed or edited — it's entirely automatic and invisible
In the Report Parameter Properties dialog's Default Values tab
questions.explain: The Dataset Properties dialog's Parameters tab lists each query parameter (like @StoreID) alongside the expression supplying its value, typically [@StoreID].

questions.q: What does the Parameter Value entry [@ReportYear] actually mean?
options: Shorthand for =Parameters!ReportYear.Value
A literal string that gets inserted into the query as-is
A reference to a field in the report's main dataset
A comment that Report Builder ignores at runtime
questions.explain: [@ReportYear] is simple syntax shorthand for the full expression =Parameters!ReportYear.Value — the report parameter's current value.

questions.q: What is the correct T-SQL WHERE clause for a single-value parameter named @StoreID?
options: WHERE StoreID = (@StoreID)
WHERE StoreID IN (@StoreID)
WHERE StoreID LIKE (@StoreID)
WHERE StoreID BETWEEN (@StoreID)
questions.explain: For a single-value parameter, the equals operator compares the column against the one value the reader chose.

questions.q: Once that same parameter becomes multi-value, what must the WHERE clause become?
options: WHERE StoreID IN (@StoreID)
It stays exactly WHERE StoreID = (@StoreID)
WHERE StoreID = ANY(@StoreID) — SQL Server doesn't support IN with parameters
The WHERE clause must be removed entirely
questions.explain: IN tests the column against a set of values, which is what a multi-value parameter supplies — this mirrors the change covered in Lesson 15.

questions.q: What makes SSRS's use of @ParameterName syntax different from writing a parameterized query in application code?
options: The mapping between the query placeholder and the parameter's value is managed visually, through the Report Data pane and Dataset Properties dialog, with no procedural glue code
SSRS doesn't actually support real T-SQL syntax like WHERE and IN
The @ symbol means something entirely different in SSRS than in T-SQL
Report parameters can only ever supply hardcoded values, never reader input
questions.explain: The SQL syntax itself is ordinary — what's distinct is that connecting the report parameter to the query placeholder is entirely visual/declarative, not something you write runtime code to wire up.
